records.place: Manduria and Sava, province of Taranto, Salento, Puglia

wine.name: Es
wine.appellation: Salento IGT, Primitivo di Manduria DOC in early vintages
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the tier below DOC
wine.grapes: Primitivo alone, from old bush vines the family owns.
wine.sites: Old alberello bush vines of Primitivo in the countryside of Manduria and Sava, on red, calcareous clay; the house began in 2004 with a single small plot of old bush vines.
wine.making: Picked by hand with close selection of the bunches, the grapes are macerated on their skins for two to three weeks in stainless steel. The wine then ages for about nine months in small oak barrels, part of them new, and rests some months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black fig, black cherry jam and liquorice with cocoa and clove; full bodied, warm and high in alcohol, yet held upright by fresh acidity and a salty, savoury finish, with ripe, smooth tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous and open from release, it keeps and gains savoury depth for some years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Freud's word for the id, the instinctive part of the mind, as the house explains the name.
The broad indication of the Salento's three provinces, carried by later vintages in place of the Manduria DOC.
The grape, named for ripening early, and the same vine as California's Zinfandel.

records.table: Es is Gianfranco Fino's Primitivo from old bush vines around Manduria and Sava, named after Freud's word for the id. Dense with black fig and liquorice, high in alcohol yet fresh and salty, it wants a large glass and a rich dish.
records.story: For a century Puglia sent much of its wine, Primitivo among it, north by the tanker to be blended into others; the Primitivo di Manduria DOC was created in 1974. Gianfranco Fino is a young house of that zone. In 2004 its founder, who had worked for years in olive growing, and his wife bought a single small plot of old Primitivo bush vines near Manduria, and Es was first made from that vintage, by the house's account. The couple went on to save more small plots of old alberello vines between Manduria and Sava from grubbing up, vines thought too poor in yield to keep. The name is Freud's: Es is the German word for the id, the instinctive part of the mind, and the house speaks of instinct and passion. Within a few vintages the Italian wine guides were praising it, and a dense Primitivo of old vines and low yields from the Salento had shown that the grape could make a wine for the cellar. Its early vintages were labelled Primitivo di Manduria DOC; later ones carry the Salento IGT, though the grapes grow around Manduria and Sava as before. For a sommelier, Es is the bottle that argues for Primitivo as a fine wine, and a reminder that a serious Puglian red may carry the broad Salento indication.

others.name: Jo
others.note: Negroamaro from the Manduria countryside on clay and limestone, the house's other red grape, labelled Salento IGT.

others.name: Sé
others.note: Another Primitivo of the house from the same countryside, also labelled Salento IGT.

others.name: Gf
others.note: A sparkling rosé of Negroamaro made by the traditional method, with its second fermentation in bottle.

traps: Later vintages of Es are labelled Salento IGT, not Primitivo di Manduria DOC, though the grapes come from the Manduria countryside as before.
Es is Primitivo; the house's Negroamaro is Jo, so do not file the two together.
Es is a dry red; the Primitivo di Manduria DOCG is the sweet Dolce Naturale, a different wine.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35; the group's one fetch, the house's Es sheet on gianfrancofino.it, was refused (the host does not resolve here), so the house's pages were read through search.

Library and plan tension: p-gianfranco-fino gives the sub zone as Primitivo di Manduria DOC and the plan's why calls Es the Primitivo di Manduria, but the house's own page and sheet class Es as Salento Primitivo IGT; Falstaff lists the 2012 to 2015 vintages as Primitivo di Manduria DOC (the 2013 a Riserva) and the 2016 (vino.com), 2019 and 2023 as Salento IGT.

Left out for want of agreement: the year and the reason of the move out of the DOC (Vinous says the founder left it in 2014 over rules he found lax, 85 per cent Primitivo with any other grape, against Falstaff's DOC 2015), so the record says early and later vintages.

Left out on one source each: Es at the G8 summit of 2008, the guide's grower of the year of 2010, a founding membership of an Accademia dell'Alberello, the new cellar and resort of 2021 at Manduria, unfined and unfiltered, and the barrels of 228 litres; vine ages run from about 40 to 100 years across sources and are left out.

The founder's training differs (an agronomist who had worked in olive growing in Gambero Rosso 2011 and Superiore.de, an oenologist from the Locorotondo school in Corriere della Sera 2012), so the story keeps only the olive growing; the year of the first Es is 2004 on the house's page and in Gambero Rosso, while Corriere says six thousand bottles in 2006, perhaps the first release.
Living names met, none in the fragment's prose save the house's own name: the founder Gianfranco Fino and his wife Simona Natale, for people.json.

records.place: Andria, Castel del Monte, the Murge, northern Puglia

wine.name: Il Falcone
wine.appellation: Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva DOCG
wine.classification: DOCG since 2011; a Riserva of the Castel del Monte DOC before
wine.grapes: Nero di Troia, some seven parts in ten, with Montepulciano for the rest.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the Murge hills around Andria in the Castel del Monte zone, at about 200 metres, on deep calcareous soils with tufa.
wine.making: Macerated for about two weeks in large stainless steel vats with daily pumping over, the wine ages fourteen months or more in French oak, part in casks of thirty hectolitres and part in barriques and tonneaux, then about a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Red and black cherry with violets, dried herbs, a little liquorice and cedar from the oak; medium to full bodied, with firm, stony tannin and fresh acidity, more upright than the reds of the Salento.
wine.ageing: Firm in its first years, it softens with some years in bottle and keeps for many more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The falcon, for the emperor Frederick II, who built Castel del Monte and loved falconry.
The DOCG of 2011 for a red led by Nero di Troia, aged two years, one in wood.

label.term: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
label.means: Italy's controlled and guaranteed designation, the tier above DOC.

records.table: Rivera's Il Falcone is the Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva of Andria: Nero di Troia with some Montepulciano, aged over a year in French oak and another in bottle. Firm, fresh and scented with violets, it shows the cooler north of Puglia, so give a young bottle air.
records.story: The de Corato family farmed the countryside of Andria in the nineteenth century, and in 1921 its patriarch bought the Rivera estate, which had belonged for centuries to a noble family of that name from Abruzzo, and made it a model farm of vines and olives. His youngest son founded the winery in the estate's old cellars in the late 1940s, and the house also gives 1950 as its start. In the commune of Andria stands Castel del Monte, the octagonal castle that the emperor Frederick II (1194 to 1250) had built on the Murge from about 1240; he wrote a treatise on hunting with birds. The Castel del Monte DOC was created in 1971, and with that vintage the house first made Il Falcone, named in his honour. In the 1970s the founder's son led trials in the vineyards and a modernised cellar. In 2011 the Riserva of the zone's red was raised to a DOCG of its own, Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva, which asks for Nero di Troia to lead, and Il Falcone has carried the new name since. For a sommelier it is the wine that shows Puglia is more than Primitivo and Negroamaro: Nero di Troia from the high ground of the north, firm, fresh and long lived.

others.name: Puer Apuliae
others.note: The house's Nero di Troia on its own, bottled under the Castel del Monte DOCG tier.

traps: The Montepulciano in Il Falcone is the grape, the red of Abruzzo, not the Tuscan town of Vino Nobile.
Castel del Monte Rosso Riserva has been a DOCG only since 2011; older vintages of Il Falcone were Riservas of the Castel del Monte DOC.
Nero di Troia, also written Uva di Troia, is a different grape from Sicily's Nero d'Avola.

cards.back: The emperor Frederick II, who built Castel del Monte nearby and loved falconry.

cards.front: With which vintage was Rivera's red first called Il Falcone, and what else began that year?

The emperor Frederick II's falconers

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share, three of them on the castle (the Ministry of Culture's page dates its first record to 1240), its builder's dates (Wikipedia's page on his treatise and a history site) and the DOC's year of 1971 (Wein.plus and others).
Library tension: p-rivera's founded 1950 is kept, as the lint asks; the house's family page says its youngest son founded the winery in the late 1940s and another of its pages says since 1950.

The first vintage of Il Falcone, 1971, is on the house's page and in a published vertical tasting; that the red was sold as a Rosso Stravecchio from 1950, and the move from cement to steel in 1988 and to small oak with the 1995, rest on that tasting alone and are left out.

The house's sheets differ by vintage on the oak (the 2018 half in casks of 30 hectolitres and half in barriques and tonneaux, the 2017 in barriques, the current page at least 16 months), so the making says fourteen months or more in French oak.
Not found: the founder's dates, so he is the patriarch's youngest son; the founder's son who led the trials of the 1970s and the fourth generation are living and not named.

Living names met, for people.json: Carlo de Corato and his sons Sebastiano and Marco de Corato, as the house's family page names them; the founder of the late 1940s, Sebastiano de Corato, is not dated in any source read and is not named.

records.place: Salice Salentino, province of Lecce, Salento, Puglia

wine.name: Five Roses
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the tier below DOC
wine.grapes: Negroamaro, the great majority, with a little Malvasia Nera.
wine.sites: Negroamaro and Malvasia Nera of the Salento around Salice Salentino, the house's home in the province of Lecce, where iron rich red clay over limestone colours the land.
wine.making: The grapes are chilled and left on their skins for some hours at about 10 degrees, then only the free run juice, the must flower, is drawn off. It ferments cool in stainless steel and rests at least two months in steel and a month in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Coral pink; wild strawberry, red cherry and pomegranate with a hint of bitter orange and wild herbs; dry, fresh and light in body, with a gently bitter, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two of the vintage, while its fruit is fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The house's name for its rosé since 1943, after a family property, as it tells it.
Italian for rosé, made from black grapes with a short time on the skins.
The indication of the Salento peninsula's three provinces, Lecce, Brindisi and Taranto.

records.table: Five Roses is Leone de Castris's rosato from Salice Salentino, Negroamaro with a little Malvasia Nera, first bottled in 1943 and told by the house as the first rosé bottled in Italy. Coral pink, dry and fresh, with cherry and bitter orange, pour it cold.
records.story: Leone de Castris dates itself to 1665, when, by the family's account, a duke of the Counts of Lemos settled at Salice Salentino and began to make wine there. Its wine was long sold in bulk, much of it abroad, until in 1925 the couple who then ran the house began to bottle it. In 1943, in the war years, came the bottling the house tells as the first rosé bottled and sold in Italy. The story, as the family tells it, turns on the Allies: Charles Poletti (1903 to 2002), a former governor of New York then serving with the Allied military government in Italy, asked for a large supply of rosé, and the wine was given, in the house's words, an American name. Five Roses comes from a family property, so called, the house says, because for several generations each de Castris had five children. In 1993, for the fiftieth anniversary, the house added Five Roses Anniversario from older vines. For a sommelier, Five Roses is the date to know for Italian rosato, 1943, and the proof that Negroamaro makes a pale, dry pink as readily as a dark red.

others.name: Five Roses Anniversario
others.note: First made in 1993 for the fiftieth anniversary, from older vines of Negroamaro and Malvasia Nera.

others.name: Donna Lisa Salice Salentino Riserva
others.note: The house's Riserva of the Salice Salentino DOC, Negroamaro with a little Malvasia Nera.

traps: Five Roses is labelled Salento IGT, not Salice Salentino DOC, although the house stands in Salice Salentino.
Its claim to be the first rosé bottled and sold in Italy, in 1943, is the house's own: give it as the house's account.
Five Roses is Negroamaro with Malvasia Nera, not Primitivo, the grape of Manduria and Gioia del Colle.

cards.front: Leone de Castris: in which year was Five Roses first bottled?
cards.back: 1943; the house tells it as the first rosé bottled and sold in Italy.

cards.front: Which grapes go into Five Roses?
cards.back: Negroamaro, the great majority, with a little Malvasia Nera.

questions.q: Leone de Castris leaves the chilled grapes for Five Roses on their skins for some hours. What happens next?
opts: Only the free run juice is drawn off and fermented
The wine is aged for a year in new oak barrels
Red and white wine are blended before bottling
The juice ferments on the skins for several weeks
questions.exp: After a short, cold maceration the house draws off the must flower, the free run juice, and ferments it in steel: a rosé of short skin contact, not a blend of red and white, and it rests in steel, not oak.

questions.q: The story of Five Roses in 1943 turns on an American officer of the Allied military government. Who was he?
opts: Charles Poletti, a former governor of New York
George Patton, general of the Seventh Army
Mark Clark, commander of the Fifth Army
Dwight Eisenhower, the Allied commander
questions.exp: By the house's account Charles Poletti asked for a large supply of rosé; he had briefly been governor of New York in 1942 before serving in the Allied military government in Italy.

sources.title: Leone de Castris: Five Roses, its story

Superiore.de: Leone de Castris, 360 years from the Salento

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share; the house is not in the library, so every fact rests on the house's own pages or two others.

The plan's note is answered: 1665 and 1943 are the house's own dates on its history and Five Roses pages, with Superiore.de and others beside them, and the first bottled rosé is given as the house's claim throughout.

The house calls Poletti a general and its supply officer; Wikipedia, the National Governors Association and the Liberation Route give him as a colonel of the Allied military government, governor of New York in December 1942, so the record gives no rank. His wish for an American name is in the house's own words and in secondary accounts; the family's own telling of a birthday party in January 1944 is left out.

Left out: the name of the duke of 1665 (the house gives Oronzo Arcangelo Maria Francesco, with no dates), the couple of 1925 by name (Piero Leone Plantera and Lisetta de Castris, undated), the Salice Salentino DOC's year, which one source gives as 1971 against the region record's 1976, and the house's part in it.

The house's sheets differ on the maceration (10 to 12 hours and at most 35 per cent drawn off on the 2022 sheet, a few hours and half on the current page), so the making says some hours; Five Roses Anniversario of 1993 rests on two merchants' pages.

Region record: its producers line for the house says Five Roses made Salice Salentino a name abroad and that the estate was founded in 1665; the record keeps 1665 as the house's account and gives Five Roses as Salento IGT, not Salice Salentino.

records.place: Guagnano, province of Lecce, Salento, Puglia

wine.name: Patriglione
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Protetta, the tier below DOC
wine.grapes: Negroamaro alone, by the house's present sheet, from old bush vines.
wine.sites: Old alberello vines of Negroamaro, some eighty years old by the house's account, in the Patriglione district of Guagnano in the north of the Salento, which gives the wine its name.
wine.making: Picked late, towards the end of October, after some of the bunches have been left to shrivel on the vine, the grapes are fermented and the wine is aged in small French oak barrels, then rests in glass lined tanks before bottling, by the house's account.
wine.glass: Dried plum, black cherry and fig with tobacco, liquorice and a bitter edge of dark chocolate and wild herbs; full bodied and warm from the shrivelled grapes, with soft but present tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Built for keeping by its late picked fruit, it needs some years in bottle and then keeps for many more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The district of Guagnano where the old bush vines grow, by the house's account.
The protected geographical indication of the Salento, the same tier as the older IGT.
The black bitter grape of the Salento, as its name is often read.

records.table: Patriglione is Cosimo Taurino's Negroamaro from old bush vines at Guagnano, picked late with some bunches shrivelled on the vine and aged in French oak. Dark and warm, with dried plum and a bitter herbal edge, it wants a decanter when it is old.
records.story: Cosimo Taurino, who died in 1999, was a pharmacist by profession and, by the house's account, gave up that career against his family's wishes to return to the family farm at Guagnano, in the north of the Salento. In 1970 he bottled Notarpanaro, a Negroamaro named for the district where its vines grow, and the house counts that bottling as the start of its life as a wine estate. In 1975, after meeting the oenologist with whom he would work, he made what the house calls a great wager on the old bush vines of the Patriglione district: Negroamaro picked very late, some of it shrivelled on the vine, then raised in small French oak barrels. The first Patriglione was the 1975. In a region whose red went north in tankers to be blended into others, Patriglione was made to be kept in bottle, and it became the wine the house is known by. Since his death the family has run the estate. For a sommelier, Patriglione is a long lived Negroamaro of the Salento from late picked fruit: dense and warm, yet with the grape's bitter, herbal finish.

others.name: Notarpanaro
others.note: The house's first bottled wine, of 1970, a Negroamaro named for the district where its vines grow.

others.name: Salice Salentino Riserva
others.note: The house's red of the Salice Salentino DOC, a Riserva of the Salento's Negroamaro appellation.

traps: Patriglione's grapes shrivel on the vine and are picked late; Amarone's are picked and then dried on racks, so the two are not made the same way.
Salento IGP and Salento IGT name the same tier: IGP is the European term and IGT the older Italian one, and labels carry either.
Patriglione is Negroamaro from Guagnano, not Primitivo from Manduria.

cards.back: 1975, made with the oenologist with whom the founder worked.

cards.front: How and when are Patriglione's grapes picked?

questions.q: A guest asks why Cosimo Taurino's Patriglione tastes so dense and warm. Which reason fits?
opts: Late picking, with some bunches shrivelled on the vine
Grapes dried on racks for months after picking
A blend with Primitivo bought from Manduria
Ageing under a veil of flor in old casks
questions.exp: The house picks its old bush vine Negroamaro late, towards the end of October, after some bunches have shrivelled on the vine; drying on racks after picking is the way of Amarone.

questions.q: Before he bottled his first wine at Guagnano in 1970, what was Cosimo Taurino's profession?
opts: Pharmacist
Lawyer
Agronomist
Physician
questions.exp: By the house's account he gave up pharmacy, against his family's wishes, to return to the farm; in 1970 he bottled Notarpanaro, the house's first wine.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share; the house is not in the library, so every fact rests on the house's own pages or two others.

The plan's note is answered: the first Patriglione is the 1975 on the house's page, in the Veronelli guide it reprints and in Skurnik's account; Skurnik also says the wine began when a forgotten cask of late picked Negroamaro of 1974 was left to ferment dry, which rests on that one account and is left out.
No birth year for Cosimo Taurino was found in any source, so he keeps his death of 1999 alone (Veronelli and Skurnik).
The oenologist of 1975 is Severino Garofano in the house's pages and the Veronelli guide; his death in October 2018 rests on one source and no birth year was found, so he is described, not named.

The house's present sheet gives Negroamaro alone; whether older vintages held Malvasia Nera was not checked, and the time in oak is left without a figure (the house says aged in small French oak barrels, a merchant gives twelve months for the 2011).
The founded year is the house's own: it counts the Notarpanaro of 1970 as the start of the business, as Skurnik does; the family farm itself is older and undated.
Region record: its producers line for Taurino calls Patriglione an early cult red of the Salento, a word the brief refuses; the record says the wine the house is known by.

Living names met, for people.json: Stefano and Renata Garofano, the oenologist's children, named in Doctor Wine's profile of their own house; the Taurino family of today is not named in any source read, and nobody living is named in the fragment.

records.place: Acquaviva delle Fonti, Gioia del Colle DOC, the Murge, Puglia

wine.name: Primitivo 16 Vigneto San Benedetto
wine.grapes: Primitivo alone, from the house's own organically farmed bush vines.
wine.sites: The San Benedetto vineyard at Acquaviva delle Fonti, on the Murge plateau between Bari and Taranto: bush vines some seventy years old by the house's account, on red, iron rich soil over a layer of limestone.
wine.making: Picked by hand into crates in early September and fermented on its skins in stainless steel at a controlled temperature, the wine ages about two years in steel, with no wood, then about a year in bottle in the cellar cut into the limestone before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, black cherry and plum with dried herbs, liquorice and a stony, savoury edge; full and warm in alcohol, yet fresher than a Manduria Primitivo, with lively acidity and no taste of oak.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, some three years after the vintage, it keeps and gains savoury notes for some years more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house's name for this Primitivo of the San Benedetto vineyard, one of several numbered bottlings.
The DOC of 1987 for the Primitivo and other wines of the Murge plateau around the town.
The San Benedetto vineyard at Acquaviva delle Fonti, the wine's single source.

records.table: Polvanera's Primitivo 16 comes from old bush vines on the Murge at Acquaviva delle Fonti, in the Gioia del Colle DOC. Aged in steel and bottle with no oak, it shows the fresher, sour cherry side of Primitivo; decant it and pour it with lamb.
records.story: Polvanera is a young house of the Murge, the limestone plateau between Bari and Taranto where, as the region's history has it, Primitivo was first named in the late eighteenth century by a priest of Gioia del Colle. The farm's name means black dust, and the house ties it to the dark, iron rich soils around it and to the charcoal once made there; its manor house dates from 1820. The estate was set up in the early 2000s by its founder, an oenologist trained at the wine school of Locorotondo who drew on his father's experience of the vines. The cellar is cut some eight metres into the limestone, where the wine keeps a steady temperature as it ages. Gioia del Colle had been a DOC since 1987; Polvanera bottled its Primitivo from old bush vines, farmed organically, and named the wines by number and by vineyard, 16 from San Benedetto and 17 from Montevella. The 16 is aged in steel and bottle alone, with no wood. For a sommelier the house shows the other face of Primitivo: grown on the high Murge rather than on Manduria's coastal sand, it keeps more freshness and savour.

others.name: Polvanera 17
others.note: The house's other Primitivo of Gioia del Colle, from the Montevella vineyard at Acquaviva delle Fonti.

others.name: Polvanera 21
others.note: A passito red of dried Primitivo grapes, labelled Puglia IGT.

others.name: Minutolo
others.note: A white of the Minutolo grape, labelled Valle d'Itria IGT.

traps: Gioia del Colle Primitivo grows on the Murge plateau inland; Primitivo di Manduria comes from the Ionian coast, and the two are different DOCs.
Polvanera 16 and Polvanera 17 come from different vineyards, San Benedetto and Montevella; the number is not a vintage.
Polvanera 16 sees no oak: its two years of ageing are in stainless steel, so a vanilla note argues against it.

cards.front: Polvanera: what is notable about the cellar where its wines age?
cards.back: It is cut some eight metres into the limestone rock of the Murge, which keeps a steady temperature.
San Benedetto, at Acquaviva delle Fonti: old bush vines on red soil over limestone.

questions.q: A guest expects oak in Polvanera's Primitivo 16. How is it in fact aged?
opts: About two years in steel, then a year in bottle
Eighteen months in new French barriques
Two years in large Slavonian oak casks
A year in clay amphorae, then in bottle
questions.exp: The house ages Polvanera 16 about two years in stainless steel and about a year in bottle, with no wood; barriques and large casks play no part in it.

questions.q: Polvanera's name means black dust. What does the house say it recalls?
opts: Dark, iron rich soils and the charcoal once made there
Volcanic ash blown from the slopes of Vesuvius
The black slate of the vineyard terraces
Coal dust from a railway that crossed the farm
questions.exp: The house ties the name to the dark, iron rich soils around its farm and the charcoal once made there; the Murge is limestone, with no volcanic ash or slate.

sources.title: WineTourism: the roots of Cantine Polvanera

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share, one shared with the Gioia del Colle rules; the house is not in the library, so every fact rests on the house's own pages or two others.

The plan's note is answered in part: the house names the wine Polvanera 16 and merchants Gioia del Colle Primitivo 16 Vigneto San Benedetto, so the name field holds the plan's words with the vineyard; no source read calls the 16 or the 17 the house's flagship, and the record treats the 16 as the wine the house is known by under the thin region rule.

What the numbers mean was not found: the 16 is labelled 16 per cent in every vintage listed and the 17 16.5 per cent, so neither is said to be the alcohol; the record says only that the number is not a vintage.
Founded is left empty: merchants and WineTourism give 2002 for the house, the house's Italian page dates the farm's start to 2003, so the story says the early 2000s.

The 17's vines are over seventy years old on a merchant's note, as are the 16's on the house's own page, so no age is given for the 17; the vineyard's altitude was not found and the story leans on the region record's Murge at around 300 to 500 metres.
No swap is proposed: the house is real, of the appellation and makes the wine; Cantine San Marzano's Sessantanni stays the plan's alternative should the checker judge the pick too thin.
Living names met, for people.json: the founder Filippo Cassano and his father Vincenzo Cassano, named on the house's page; neither is named in the fragment.
